notes.meaning: Jesus promises that some of the people standing with him will not die before they see God's kingdom come with power. Most early church writers and traditional commentators saw this fulfilled in the Transfiguration, where Jesus revealed his royal glory to three disciples. Others also see it pointing forward to his resurrection and the pouring out of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

differ.view: Some teach that Jesus was referring primarily to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman army in AD 70.
Some hold that Jesus meant certain people present would live to see the beginning of the final judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often debate four possible fulfillments: the Transfiguration, the resurrection and ascension, Pentecost, or the second coming, though many favor the Transfiguration.

notes.meaning: Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain to pray and be alone with God. While there, he was transfigured, which means his outward appearance changed so that his divine glory shone through. He gave them this preview of his majesty to strengthen their faith before they had to watch him suffer and die on the cross.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The light seen on the mountain was God's uncreated divine nature itself, which opened the disciples' eyes to see Christ as he truly is and revealed what transformed humanity will become.

notes.meaning: The clothes of Jesus began to shine with an intense, dazzling brightness. Mark explains that no cleaner on earth could ever bleach fabric that white, showing this pure light was heavenly. The shining radiance began within Jesus himself and spread outward to his clothing.

Moses and Elijah suddenly appeared on the mountain and spoke with Jesus. Moses represented God's Law and Elijah represented the Prophets, showing that all the ancient Scriptures point to Christ. Because Moses had died and Elijah had been taken to heaven alive, their appearance also showed Christ's authority over both the dead and the living.

Overwhelmed by the wonder of the moment, Peter suggested building three shelters out of branches so they could stay on the mountain. He loved being in Christ's holy presence and wished this heavenly experience would never end. However, his idea mistakenly put Moses and Elijah on the same level as Jesus and forgot the people waiting in need below.

Peter spoke impulsively because all three disciples were overcome with deep awe and dread. Catching a glimpse of the heavenly world brought a trembling fear to their human hearts. Peter felt compelled to speak, even though he did not really know what was appropriate to say.

A bright cloud of God's presence surrounded them, and the Father spoke directly from heaven. The Father announced that Jesus is his dearly loved Son and commanded them to listen to him. This command showed that Christ is greater than Moses and Elijah, serving as God's ultimate messenger and King.

As soon as the heavenly voice spoke, the cloud, Moses, and Elijah vanished. The disciples looked around in astonishment and found only Jesus with them in his normal appearance. This shows that while special spiritual moments come and go, Jesus remains with his people always.

As they walked down the mountain, Jesus ordered the disciples not to tell anyone what they had witnessed until he had risen from the dead. Spreading the story too early would cause misunderstandings while he was still walking the humble road toward the cross. Once he conquered death, the memory of his transfiguration would serve as powerful proof that he was the risen Lord.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The apostles were told to wait because they had seen Christ's risen glory in advance, so the vision could only be rightly understood after his passion and death.

notes.meaning: The disciples kept the event to themselves as commanded, but they were deeply puzzled by the idea of rising from the dead. They already believed in the general resurrection of all people at the end of time, but they could not understand how the Messiah himself would die and rise first. They still expected him to set up an earthly kingdom without suffering.

The disciples asked Jesus about the scribes' teaching that Elijah must return before the Messiah comes. Since Elijah had just appeared and then quickly vanished, they wondered how this prophecy from the Old Testament had been fulfilled. They were trying to make sense of what their teachers had taught alongside what they had just seen.

Jesus affirmed that Elijah was meant to come first to prepare the people and restore spiritual order. Then he pointed them to other Scriptures showing that the Son of Man was appointed to suffer terrible pain and rejection. He wanted them to see that the Messiah's glory could not be separated from his suffering on the cross.

Jesus explained that the promised forerunner had indeed arrived in the person of John the Baptist. Wicked leaders had mistreated and executed John, acting out the same hatred that past rulers had shown toward the prophets. In doing so, they previewed the violent suffering that Jesus himself would soon endure.

Coming down to the other nine disciples, Jesus found a large crowd and scribes arguing with them. The religious teachers were challenging the disciples because they had failed to cast an evil spirit out of a young boy. The enemies of Jesus used this failure to embarrass his followers and question his authority.

When the crowd saw Jesus approaching, they were filled with sudden awe and ran to welcome him. His arrival was unexpected and perfectly timed to bring order to the chaos. Some commentators suggest that a lingering trace of heavenly brightness on his face may have added to their amazement.

Jesus stepped into the middle of the crowd to defend his disciples and asked the scribes what they were arguing about. He took command of the situation immediately and brought the debate to a halt. His presence silenced his critics, who did not dare repeat their challenges to him directly.

A father in the crowd spoke up to explain why everyone was gathered and arguing. He had brought his suffering son to Jesus because the boy was tormented by an evil spirit that made him unable to speak. Hoping to find the Master, the father had arrived only to find the nine disciples.

The father described how the spirit threw the boy into violent convulsions, making him foam at the mouth, grind his teeth, and waste away. He had asked the disciples to drive the demon out, but they did not have the power to do it. Their inability left the father crushed with disappointment and gave the scribes an excuse to mock.

Jesus lamented the lack of faith in the people around him, including the crowd, the scribes, and his own disciples. He grieved over how long he had walked among them while their hearts remained slow to trust God's power. Yet despite his sorrow over their unbelief, he graciously told them to bring the boy to him.

When the boy was brought forward, the evil spirit saw Jesus and immediately threw the child into a violent seizure. The boy fell to the ground, rolling around and foaming at the mouth. Knowing its time was short, the demon staged a desperate, furious final assault in the presence of the Savior.

Jesus asked the father how long the child had suffered in this condition, and the father replied that it had gone on since childhood. Jesus asked this question not to gain information, but to reveal how desperate and long-standing the boy's affliction was. By drawing out these details, Jesus helped prepare the father and the crowd for the miracle to come.

The father explained that the demon had often tried to kill the boy by throwing him into fire and water. Worn down by years of suffering and the disciples' failure, he begged Jesus to have pity and help if he had the power to do anything. His plea showed a father's deep love for his child, but it also revealed lingering doubt about whether Jesus could heal him.

Jesus repeated the father's words back to him to show that the real issue was not God's power, but human faith. He declared that all things are possible for the person who trusts in God. True faith relies completely on God's limitless strength, opening the way for his power to accomplish what seems impossible.

The father cried out in tears, admitting both his sincere trust and the doubt that still troubled his mind. He asked Jesus to help him overcome his lack of faith, refusing to hide his spiritual struggle. This honest cry shows that even small, struggling faith can cast itself upon Christ for rescue and strength.

Seeing the crowd rushing forward, Jesus acted immediately to end the public spectacle and deliver the child. Addressing the spirit directly as a real and separate evil power, he commanded it to come out and never enter the boy again. Christ showed his absolute authority by commanding a complete and permanent deliverance.
